title: Can ARIA turn bold science into benefits for Britain?
label: 8 September 2026 · ARIA's progress and challenges
summary: The committee questioned Dr Kathleen Fisher, the new head of the Advanced Research and Invention Agency (ARIA), about its publicly funded, high-risk research. Fisher described promising early results and argued that even projects that miss their ultimate goals can produce useful discoveries and companies. Members pressed her on how ARIA judges failure, avoids duplicating other research, attracts talent and helps inventions become real products. The sharpest disagreements concerned whether discoveries funded in Britain will actually create jobs and wealth there, why funding remains concentrated in the south-east, and how conflicts of interest are handled. Fisher defended ARIA's approach while acknowledging that regional reach and the route from research to practical benefit still need work. She warned that truly transformative results may take decades.

glossary.definition: The UK's Advanced Research and Invention Agency, which funds ambitious research that may fail but could produce major breakthroughs.
A US government agency that funds ambitious research, mainly for national security, and helped inspire ARIA.
Specialists hired by ARIA to design research programmes, choose teams and decide how projects should change or end.
Organisations hired to help ARIA-funded researchers with practical needs such as engineering, starting companies or attracting investors.
Artificial intelligence: computer systems that perform tasks such as analysing information or generating answers.
Money invested in young companies with high growth potential, usually in exchange for a share of ownership.
Legal rights over inventions and other creations, which can be owned, licensed or sold.
The concentration of major research institutions around London, Oxford and Cambridge in south-east England.
UK Research and Innovation, the public organisation that funds a broad range of research and research facilities.
The National Health Service, the UK's publicly funded healthcare system.
The body's broad, immediate defence against germs, rather than a response tailored to a particular infection.
The part of the body's defences that learns to recognise and target particular germs, as vaccines help it do.

chapters.title: A bold mission, with early results
chapters.takeaway: ARIA wants breakthroughs with lasting public benefit, and Fisher says smaller successes matter even when the biggest goal isn't reached.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You became ARIA's chief executive in February. What are your priorities now that the agency is getting established?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We have more than 300 researchers and other creators working across 15 programmes. We have £1.2 billion allocated for the current spending period, and my job is to turn that funding into results. Real success isn't how much we spend. It's breakthroughs in science, benefits for society and the economy, and a greater willingness to attempt ambitious research.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Some projects will miss their extraordinary goals, but still teach us something important. We also need to make sure discoveries actually reach people, rather than sitting unused for decades. We've appointed a senior executive specifically to help researchers turn results into practical benefits.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Which current projects show what you mean?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: One project is trying to give early warning of major climate changes, including shifts in Atlantic ocean currents and melting in Greenland. A Plymouth company, Oshen, is developing small, low-cost, self-powered sea robots to gather ocean measurements. It began with one and has deployed five, with plans for 50.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: The US weather agency then asked Oshen to try measuring conditions inside a powerful hurricane. That was risky, but its robots successfully sent back information during a category 5 storm. The company has since won contracts with five governments. Even if our original climate-warning goal proves impossible, this technology could still be valuable.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We also employ activation partners to remove obstacles for research teams. Amodo Design in Sheffield built batteries that work at minus 50 degrees for sensors in Greenland. The researchers thought the usual funding and procurement process would take at least 18 months. Amodo did the work in three months, and the design may help 11 other teams.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: These are useful results, but ARIA's biggest breakthroughs may take a decade or more. I worked at DARPA, the US agency that inspired this approach, and I've seen how powerful it can be if researchers have freedom, sustained backing and permission to take risks.

chapters.title: When to persist, change course or stop
chapters.takeaway: Projects are reviewed regularly, but ARIA expects plans to change and requires fresh justification before extending funding.

turns.speaker: Baroness Willis of Summertown
turns.text: How can you tell whether so many risky projects are progressing, especially when most grants last only a few years?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Each programme sets its own goals and measures of progress. Programme directors talk with their research teams every three months. We check both the science and whether the results could be put to use. Outside experts review programmes annually, and we can add funding, change direction or stop a project that isn't working.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: For example, part of our AI safety programme aimed to check whether AI systems themselves behaved reliably. Given how quickly the technology is changing, the team judged that approach unworkable and shifted the money to using AI alongside mathematical checks to test important infrastructure instead.

turns.speaker: Baroness Willis of Summertown
turns.text: How do you make sure you're funding work that wouldn't happen anyway? And should we judge ARIA by a few extraordinary successes, even if many projects fail?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We ask whether a proposed project is genuinely different and whether somebody else would do it without us. If no researchers work in an area, there may be nobody able to deliver. If everyone is already working on it, ARIA probably isn't needed. Over decades, there may be rare breakthroughs large enough to justify many years of funding, but smaller advances and new companies count too.

turns.speaker: Baroness Willis of Summertown
turns.text: But isn't three years too short for serious research? Can you keep funding the same field or the same outstanding scientist?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Programmes usually last three to five years. They can continue, but not automatically: we must actively decide that more ARIA funding is still needed. DARPA backed AI for 60 years through repeated new decisions, not a single 60-year promise. We can support the same person again if their next work fits our purpose, though ARIA is still too young to know how often that will happen.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We can also speed things up. A Newcastle researcher expected his sensor work to take three years while working one day a week. We funded him to spend four days a week on it, and he achieved the original three-year plan in one year. That doesn't mean his funding just stops; he can go further.

turns.speaker: Lord Duncan of Springbank
turns.text: What if a project won't reach its original target but reveals another promising direction?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: The director and researchers can change course if the new work still serves the programme's purpose. We're making contracts more flexible so worthwhile changes don't require months of paperwork. We can still measure progress separately from the contract.

chapters.title: Choosing the people and the funding approach
chapters.takeaway: ARIA gives programme directors broad freedom, but expects them to combine scientific judgement, leadership and a practical plan for results.

turns.speaker: Lord Winston
turns.text: Programme directors have extraordinary freedom. What qualities matter when choosing the next group?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: They need strong science knowledge across different fields, sound judgement about ambitious claims, and the ability to persuade and lead other people. They also need to think about how discoveries reach users, handle setbacks and learn from feedback. Nobody arrives with every skill. Their appointments are usually three years, with a possible extension of one or two.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We're recruiting our third group. More than 1,200 people had applied when I last checked, against 400 in the previous round. The first group leaned towards university researchers; the second towards entrepreneurs. We want a mix, and we're again allowing some directors to work four days a week so academics can keep supervising students.

turns.speaker: Lord Patel
turns.text: Does it matter whether they come from universities or industry?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Both can succeed. A mixture helps because the directors learn from one another.

turns.speaker: Lord Winston
turns.text: Your predecessor suggested the best projects split expert opinion almost equally between enthusiasm and disbelief. Do you agree?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Not necessarily fifty-fifty. If everyone thinks the idea is excellent, it may already be established enough to happen without us. If nobody thinks it has merit, that's worrying too. We want a serious but uncertain possibility, not disagreement just for its own sake.

turns.speaker: Lord Winston
turns.text: How do directors decide who gets the research funding?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: It depends on the science. With slow-growing plants, we fund work from the start because rushing won't make plants grow faster. For high-altitude communications vehicles, we back several competing designs and stop the least promising ones, though that can discourage teams from cooperating. Other programmes use an initial research phase before choosing the next projects, or a competition with carefully designed rules.

chapters.title: Will British-funded inventions benefit Britain?
chapters.takeaway: Fisher prioritises getting inventions used and helping companies survive, while Drayson questions whether that adequately protects the UK's economic return.

turns.speaker: Lord Drayson
turns.text: ARIA must bring economic benefits to the UK. How will it do that rather than simply create useful inventions for the whole world?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: A breakthrough can save Britain money even without profits. Our work on brain and nervous-system conditions could, if successful, reduce NHS costs and help people return to work. We're also supporting researchers who want to start businesses and make their discoveries available to customers.

turns.speaker: Lord Drayson
turns.text: But those health benefits could happen anywhere. What's to stop the companies, jobs and profits going abroad?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: The first challenge is getting an invention out of the laboratory and into use; many never make it. We want Britain to be an attractive place to start and grow these companies. Our activation partners help scientists find investors, build businesses and see an unsuccessful first start-up as useful experience, rather than the end of a career.

turns.speaker: Lord Drayson
turns.text: Why use American investment organisations for some of that work? Shouldn't British investors have priority?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Those overseas partners must set up UK operations and invest the agreed funds here. British investment would be welcome, but if an American investor helps a promising business survive and stay in the UK, that's welcome too. The company's survival and its decision to remain here matter more than the investor's nationality.

turns.speaker: Lord Drayson
turns.text: Our previous inquiry found that promising British technology companies often leave. Couldn't these partners end up helping overseas investors acquire the best discoveries instead of building wealth here?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: I don't see that as a huge risk compared with the benefit of their expertise. ARIA can help create strong companies, but other parts of the UK economy also have to make staying attractive. We can't guarantee every business will remain here.

turns.speaker: Lord Drayson
turns.text: What about intellectual property? Why doesn't ARIA keep ownership of inventions paid for with public money? Have you considered changing that?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We generally leave ownership with the inventors so it's easier for them to raise venture capital and build companies. Most are in the UK. If those rights are licensed, transferred or sold abroad, a payment is due under our terms. We've discussed changing the policy, but so far we think it gives discoveries their best chance of reaching people.

turns.speaker: Lord Drayson
turns.text: So you're reviewing the idea, but haven't decided to change the policy?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Correct. We will change it if we find a better approach, but our present judgement is to keep it.

chapters.title: Conflicts of interest and an uneven funding map
chapters.takeaway: Members challenged both ARIA's governance and the concentration of its funding in the south-east, while Fisher defended its safeguards and promised wider outreach.

turns.speaker: Lord Ranger of Northwood
turns.text: Matt Clifford was going to join the American AI company Anthropic while remaining ARIA's chair, before announcing his resignation yesterday. Many UK AI businesses saw a serious conflict of interest. Why was that arrangement considered acceptable?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: ARIA wasn't consulted. Appointing the chair and deciding how to handle that potential conflict were matters for the government department responsible, not ARIA's executive team. I did hear the same critical reaction that you've described.

turns.speaker: Lord Patel
turns.text: What lesson should be learned? Surely a future chair mustn't have interests that undermine ARIA's work.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Absolutely. But board members are chosen partly for their knowledge of the industries involved, so some overlapping interests are inevitable. They must declare those interests publicly, and we monitor them and put safeguards in place. It's a balance between expertise and conflicts that could interfere with the agency.

turns.speaker: Lord Booth
turns.text: In 2025–26, 67% of your funding went to the 'golden triangle' around London and the south-east, barely changed from 66% the previous year. What are you doing to reach the rest of the UK?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We do support strong teams elsewhere, including in Plymouth, Sheffield and Newcastle, but we're not where we want to be. Before a new programme is approved, its director now has to identify relevant researchers across all UK nations and regions and speak to a representative range of them. We're working with scientific advisers in Scotland and Northern Ireland, and reaching out to Wales too.

turns.speaker: Baroness Jones of Whitchurch
turns.text: Talking to researchers isn't the same as giving them funding. The figures haven't improved. How will you stop awards going to the same familiar institutions?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We need to find people who don't yet know how to work with ARIA, or don't believe we'd fund them. We're also improving our figures: they currently record only organisations contracted directly by us, not the smaller teams those organisations pay. We'll track applicants and where the money eventually goes, so we can see whether people aren't applying or aren't being selected.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Another advantage is that ARIA can pay the full cost of approved research, so less wealthy universities aren't expected to contribute their own money. I want to try these changes without weakening our priority of selecting the best research.

turns.speaker: Baroness Jones of Whitchurch
turns.text: Meanwhile, about 15% of funding goes outside the UK—more than some British regions receive. Why allow that?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We can fund up to 20% abroad, but each overseas award must meet a tougher test: it must provide expertise we can't get in the UK and significantly improve a programme's chances. Most work should be done here. Sometimes foreign teams move here as a result; one company relocated to London and invested more than the ARIA grant it received.

chapters.title: Finding genuinely new research
chapters.takeaway: ARIA combines wide consultation, independent checks and cautious use of AI to avoid funding ideas that are already being pursued elsewhere.

turns.speaker: Lord Stern of Brentford
turns.text: How do programme directors discover who's working on an idea and whether their proposed research would add something new?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: They read research, use AI to help survey it, and speak to scientists across Britain and abroad. They publish their proposed direction for comment and bring experts from different fields together in workshops. The resulting plan goes to ARIA leaders and outside experts for approval. The conversations often reveal possibilities that none of the individual fields had considered.

turns.speaker: Baroness Willis of Summertown
turns.text: I've attended workshops where most participants had a personal interest in getting their own field funded. Could that distort your choices? And are you duplicating major research foundations abroad?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: That's a fair concern. Workshops help us understand the science and find researchers, but participants may hope to win funding. Our formal reviewers can't apply for money from the programme they're judging. We're also using AI to read large amounts of research and challenge assumptions, though it doesn't make the decisions and we check its sources.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: What looks like duplication may have a different aim. Our new electronic smell-sensing programme, for example, wants one general-purpose detector rather than a separate device for every use. The director had spoken with researchers working on seemingly similar technology. If new evidence undermines our plans, we can change or close them.

turns.speaker: Baroness Willis of Summertown
turns.text: What if a major foundation announced almost exactly the same project?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We'd speak to them and check how much the work and the researchers actually overlap. Two approaches might both be worth funding if the problem is hard and there are enough capable teams. But paying the same people twice for essentially the same work might not be sensible. We already talk with other foundations, including the Gates Foundation.

chapters.title: Working with government and other research funders
chapters.takeaway: ARIA needs buyers and long-term scientific support, but Fisher wants government involvement timed to each project's needs.

turns.speaker: Lord Stern of Brentford
turns.text: You worked at DARPA. What's different about ARIA, and what can the UK learn from the American model?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Both let specialists lead ambitious, risky projects. DARPA serves US national security, has a much bigger budget and has existed for decades. ARIA works across science for wider public benefit. People sometimes assume DARPA has an easy route to customers in the US military, but in my experience even successful defence research needed active effort to get it used.

turns.speaker: Lord Stern of Brentford
turns.text: Could the UK government help by becoming a customer for ARIA inventions? Should departments be pushed to work with you sooner?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Yes, where a project is ready. For instance, we've supported new types of computer hardware for AI. Individual components may be fast, but customers need a complete system that works better. Our Scaling Inference Lab is bringing the hardware together, with a government commitment to buy the resulting computing system. That gives the research a potential first customer.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We've had helpful responses from departments when we've approached them. I'd welcome more engagement, while keeping ARIA free to make its own research decisions. But approaching government too early can distract from the science. The timing depends on the project.

turns.speaker: Lord Stern of Brentford
turns.text: And what about UKRI, which funds much of Britain's wider research? Should it adopt ARIA's methods?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We need a healthy UKRI. It supports researchers and facilities for the long term, while ARIA concentrates money and people on particular problems for three to five years at a time. Those approaches complement each other. I'm speaking with UKRI's leaders, but I wouldn't claim enough knowledge of its operations to prescribe how it should change.

turns.speaker: Lord Stern of Brentford
turns.text: I'd add that Britain's scientific strength also comes from centuries of universities, many of which now face financial pressures. It shouldn't all be credited to UKRI.

chapters.title: Health research and the long view
chapters.takeaway: Fisher described ambitious medical projects while stressing that ARIA's biggest scientific hopes are far from guaranteed.

turns.speaker: Lord Patel
turns.text: Could ARIA help make better use of NHS health records? They're valuable for research, but often scattered and inconsistent, and patients' information mustn't be misused.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We're already investing substantially in health research: more than £100 million in programmes involving brain and nervous-system conditions, and roughly £100 million across work on resistance to viruses and how cells produce energy. But our budget covers all science. To take on a health-data project we'd need a programme director with the right expertise, and we'd need to protect access to sensitive data and follow proper ethical safeguards.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Looking ahead, what would you most like ARIA to achieve?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Eventually, I'd love one transformative result on the scale of technologies DARPA helped make possible, such as the internet. We can't predict when that might happen. Meanwhile, I want useful discoveries, companies that turn research into benefits, and an agency that's grown from a small start-up into a well-run organisation people still want to work for.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: One example of the ambition is a project led by Brian Wang. Vaccines usually train the adaptive immune system to recognise particular viruses. He's exploring whether we can instead strengthen the innate immune system, the body's more general defences, to give around three months' protection against many respiratory viruses, possibly including common colds.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: If it worked, it might reduce illness and time off work and offer a treatment ready to use against a future pandemic. We'd want the UK to share in those benefits. But it's high-risk research and probably won't work exactly as hoped. Even an unsuccessful attempt could teach us valuable science.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: A cure for the common cold would certainly be an extraordinary achievement.
